html:
Couscous is a dish of tiny grains of rolled semolina, steamed over a stew of meat and vegetables. It is the staple dish of the Maghreb, eaten from Libya to Morocco, and has been made at least since the 1200s, when it appears in cookbooks.

It is generally thought to be a Berber invention. Making it was women's work: wheat was rolled by hand into grains, then steamed twice in a special pot. It is served on Fridays and at weddings and funerals, and every region has its own version.

North African migrants took it to France, where it became one of the most popular dishes. In 2020 Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and Mauritania jointly listed it with UNESCO as shared heritage, a rare joint act by rival states. See also Morocco and Tunisia.
